moves.spoken: This g5 lunge shows up constantly at this level — it's meant to intimidate. But the right question is: what did it weaken? Immediately the f5 square becomes a permanent hole. So the plan writes itself — steer a knight toward g3 or e3 to occupy it.
Even without a bishop to chase, the point stands: routing the knight this way is all about earning access to that f5 square. The square is the target, not any single piece.
Now the strange-looking move — the knight pulls all the way back. The end goal is simple even if the route is odd: land a knight on f5. Everything is bent toward reaching that square.
Two goals sit behind this: first, get the knight to f5; second, prise the position open, because the opponent has moved nothing but pawns. Undeveloped pieces are an invitation to open lines.
The knight steps to e3, and the earlier retreat starts to make sense — that quiet regrouping was clearing the runway for this.
Here's the puzzle: a knight dragged all the way home. Why? The hint is that it's there to support one specific pawn thrust — the piece isn't parked, it's loading a lever.
That lever is h3 — the move the retreat was preparing all along. It's the break that cracks the kingside open.
Aren't knights on the rim grim? Usually — but this one has a future, with g5 waiting for it. And the deeper win is that the position has been forced open while the opponent is still asleep.
Opening lines against such a lagging development is decisive. And the second goal lands too — the other knight is on its way to that f5 outpost.

If the outpost knight gets taken, the pawn recaptures, chases the defending knight, and can even ram down to f6. Normally you want to recapture an outpost with a piece — but there are exceptions, and this is shaping into one.

The exception is justified by how badly the opponent is developed — the whole aim is to keep the flames roaring and the position wide open. From here the search shifts to the kill, and there's already a fork in the air against a loose, undefended pawn.

It's an undefended pawn we're already making contact with, so we simply round it up. Grabbing material like this is usually greedy, but total development dominance earns the right — and it rips open the h-file, a road that could lead all the way to the king.

That pawn thrust looks menacing but folds easily — no need to defend, just push past it. The check that follows is harmless because it traps the opponent's own knight, forcing it to shuffle back and lose more time.

Now the heavy pieces join: the queen swings over to x-ray the king, the bishop develops and long castling links the rooks — full development, at last, all pointed at the enemy king. The attack itself is a knight leaping to g5, hitting f7 and threatening mate; goad the dark-square concessions, and the open h-file becomes the highway for a hook-mate finish. The opponent's whole campaign was bluff — there were never any attackers behind it.
Rewind to the critical decision: that g5 push permanently wrecked the f5 square. That single concession is what made everything afterward possible.

A piece is never bad simply because of where it sits or how few squares it seems to touch — judge it by the role it fills. A knight tucked away in the corner can be worth more than one that looks active, if its job is precise enough.

That knight's job was to prepare the h3 break and tear the h-file open. Why not just play h3 at once? Because the bishop covers h3 — push it early and the file stays shut. The regrouping was what made the break real.

There's a second reason for the retreat: if the h3 break ever gets stopped, the same knight can reroute to g3 and pair with its partner, both bearing down on f5. Sometimes you go backward to go forward — a celebrated old idea, a knight retreating to the back rank only to re-emerge on a far better path.

How do you get away with a plan this slow? Only because the opponent spent the opening shoving pawns — no firepower to punish the delay. By the time real development arrives, the cushion is more than enough to run a plan that would be far too slow in a sharper position.
